```{r}
#| label: setup
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
tab_dir <- file.path("..", "results", "tables")
fig_dir <- file.path("..", "results", "figures")
k <- function(f, digits = 3) kable(
  read_csv(file.path(tab_dir, f), show_col_types = FALSE), digits = digits)
# Slim display for contrast tables: combine the HL estimate with its CI so
# wide tables fit a portrait page without wrapping.
fmt_contrast <- function(f) {
  d <- read_csv(file.path(tab_dir, f), show_col_types = FALSE)
  d$hl <- sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", d$hl_est, d$hl_l, d$hl_u)
  keep <- c("contrast", "n_pairs", "W", "p", "p_holm", "hl", "r_rb")
  keep <- keep[keep %in% names(d)]
  out <- d[, keep]
  names(out) <- c("Contrast", "n", "W", "p", "p (Holm)", "HL [95% CI]", "r")[seq_along(keep)]
  kable(out, digits = 4)
}
```

## Abstract

Methanolic extracts of *Azadirachta indica* and *Moringa oleifera* (leaves,
stem bark, roots, seeds) were tested against *Trypanosoma congolense* and
*T. evansi* in motility assays and in albino mice (N = 16 plant × part ×
parasite blocks; group means of n = 3 mice). Both parasites responded in a
monotonic, concentration-dependent manner. *T. evansi* responded
significantly (parasitaemia Friedman p = 0.006; 100, 10 and 0.5 mg/ml each
superior to control, Holm 0.039); *T. congolense* responded suggestively
(Friedman p = 0.074; 100 mg/ml Holm 0.071). At 100 mg/ml, mean peak
parasitaemia was zero with no mortality in either parasite, against peak
LEV 5 with universal mortality in Negative Controls. The two plants were
indistinguishable (paired p = 1.0; HL 0.3, 95% CI −14.7 to 20.5). Inference
is block-level and rank-based throughout, and all headline claims withstood
leave-one-block-out sensitivity analysis.

## 1. Aim and structure of this report

The aim of the study is to compare the anti-trypanosomal activity of
methanolic extracts of *A. indica* and *M. oleifera* (leaves, stem bark,
roots, seeds) against *T. congolense* and *T. evansi* (thesis §1.8.1). This
report presents the statistical analysis for specific objectives ii–v
(§1.8.2): phytochemical characterisation (§5.2), the in-vitro motility assay
(§5.3), in-vivo infectivity (§5.4) and the superiority assessment (§5.5),
followed by diagnostics (§6), an integrative discussion (§7) and limitations
(§8). Objective i (extraction) is a laboratory procedure without recorded
replicates and carries no statistical component (§5.1).

## 2. Design and analytical approach

The source data are group means of three mice per group. Consequently, each
treatment group within a plant × part × parasite block is a single
observation, and the block (N = 16; eight per plant and per parasite) is the
unit of analysis. Plant effects are estimated from eight part × parasite
pairs; parasite effects from eight plant × part pairs. Controls are reported
as labelled in the source, their identities and doses being unstated, so the
Positive Control functions as an assay-validity reference rather than a
comparator. With at most eight pairs per test, the design has low power by
construction; effect sizes with confidence intervals are therefore reported
throughout and p-values treated as supplementary.

## 3. Endpoints

The primary parasitaemia endpoint is the death-censored AUC (trapezoidal sum
over observed days), interpreted strictly alongside mortality; peak LEV,
clearance day and day-40 status are supporting. Day-40 LEV alone is
uninformative (no group positive at day 40 against ~30% positivity at days
9–14). Motility is summarised as time-to-immobilisation, t120 motility and
mean proportion motile (source key: `+ Active`, `− No motility`; the two
`+-` cells set to NA). Weight and PCV enter as Post-minus-Pre differences
with literature-based anaemia and weight-loss flags. LEV readings above the
0–5 scale (42 cells) were capped at 5 with raw values preserved and flagged;
missing in-vivo values were taken as deaths (an adopted convention, never
imputed).

## 4. Statistical methods

All inference is rank-based: Friedman tests blocked by block for ordered dose
trends with pooled Spearman correlations on log10 dose, and paired Wilcoxon
signed-rank tests for dose-versus-control post-hoc families (Holm-adjusted
per parasite) and for plant and parasite contrasts, each accompanied by the
matched-pairs rank-biserial effect (|r| ≥ 0.11/0.28/0.43 as small/medium/
large) and the Hodges–Lehmann median difference with 95% confidence
interval. Exact p-values are used wherever the data permit; where tied ranks
or zero differences occur, the continuity-corrected normal approximation is
substituted and the substitution recorded per contrast (§6). Per-block trend
tests at n = 1 lack power, so only the blocked tests are inferential.
Computations are in `analysis/R/02_analysis.R`; no machine learning was used.

## 5.1. Objective i — methanolic extraction

No yields or replicates were recorded for the extraction step, so objective i
contributes no data to the analysis and is noted here only for completeness.

## 5.2. Objective ii — phytochemical contents

The screening panel resolved eight of twelve compound classes in at least one
extract, distributed along a part axis rather than a plant axis. Leaves were
the richest fraction in both species (6 of 12 classes each), stem bark and
roots the sparsest (3–4), and seeds intermediate (4–5; @tbl-phyto, @fig-rich).
Saponins and carbohydrates were ubiquitous (8 of 8 combinations) while
anthraquinones, phlobatannins, oxalates and phytates were uniformly absent,
so neither group discriminates the plants; tannins showed the sharpest part
pattern, present everywhere except seeds in both species (@fig-phyto-hm). The
few differentiating classes were part-specific rather than species-specific:
steroids (only *A. indica* leaves and seeds), terpenoids (only *M. oleifera*
stem bark), alkaloids, flavonoids and glucosides in asymmetric but
overlapping distributions — e.g. the two leaf profiles share six classes
apiece with only the steroid/glucoside entries swapped. With eight
combinations, these data admit description only; compound–efficacy overlays
are tabulated without tests. The substantive point for §7 is the extent of
chemical overlap between the species, which leaves little phytochemical basis
for expecting divergent efficacy.

## 5.3. Objective iii — in-vitro motility

Both parasites were immobilised in strict concentration order. Median
time-to-immobilisation lengthened monotonically from 15 minutes at 100 mg/ml
(uncensored in all blocks) to fully censored Negative Controls, with t120
motility rising from zero to 0.67 (*congolense*) and 1.0 (*evansi*) in the
controls (@tbl-tti; @fig-tti). The trajectories (@fig-mot-traj) show the
same ordering within every block, and the Positive Controls behaved as a
reference trypanocide should — motile at t = 0, immobile thereafter in all
sixteen tables — which validates the assay and establishes the benchmark
that the top extract dose reproduces. Formally, the blocked trend was highly
significant in both parasites (@tbl-mot-dose; *congolense* Friedman
Q = 27.75, p < 0.001, ρ = −0.70; *evansi* Q = 30.32, p < 0.001, ρ = −0.88).
Post-hoc contrasts against the control (@tbl-mot-posthoc) were uniformly
large at the top doses (rank-biserial −1; HL reductions of −0.83 and −0.89
at 100 mg/ml) but, with eight blocks and Holm correction, stopped just short
of significance (Holm 0.065 and 0.052; 10 mg/ml 0.085 and 0.052), and lower
doses were indistinguishable from control — several low-dose pairs matched
it exactly. The in-vitro conclusion is therefore a significant ordered trend
with large but multiplicity-limited pairwise effects, concentrated at
100 mg/ml.

## 5.4. Objective iv — in-vivo infectivity

### Parasitaemia

The in-vivo gradient reproduced the dish. Mean peak parasitaemia declined
monotonically with dose to exactly zero at 100 mg/ml in both parasites with
no deaths, against peak LEV 5 with universal mortality in the Negative
Controls (@tbl-peak; @fig-peak); mortality, clearance time and day-40
clearance all tracked the same ordering (@fig-mort), and trajectories peaked
near days 9–14 before resolving in survivors (@fig-para-traj). On cumulative
burden the *T. evansi* trend was significant (@tbl-dose; Friedman Q = 14.51,
p = 0.006, ρ = −0.51) with 100, 10 and 0.5 mg/ml each superior to control in
all eight blocks (W = 0, exact p = 0.008, Holm 0.039; HL −50/−50/−44
AUC-days), while 0.01 and 0.005 mg/ml lost significance on correction (Holm
0.078) despite strongly negative estimates. *T. congolense* showed the same
direction with weaker evidence (Friedman p = 0.074; 100 mg/ml Holm 0.071,
HL −29.9 [−41.0, −20.9]; lower doses Holm ≥ 0.32; @tbl-para-posthoc,
@fig-auc). Overall burdens did not differ between parasites (paired p = 0.46,
HL 6.0 [−10.7, 21.1]; @tbl-other): the species differ in dose sensitivity,
not in the burden the model produces.

### Body weight and PCV

Neither measure responded to treatment. Mean trajectories across the three
timepoints were flat and overlapping (@fig-wp-traj), deltas centred near
zero (@fig-wt, @fig-pcv), and no plant or parasite contrast approached
significance (@tbl-other; all p ≥ 0.15 with intervals spanning zero). The
informative signal is instead where the flags fell (@tbl-flags): deaths,
severe weight loss and anaemia concentrated almost entirely in *T.
congolense* blocks of both plants, with *T. evansi* groups largely unflagged.
Two inferences follow. First, the parasitaemia effects above are not
confounded by differential toxicity — treated groups gained no weight or PCV
advantage because there was no toxicity gradient to begin with. Second, *T.
congolense* is confirmed as the more pathogenic organism in this model,
independently of extract.

## 5.5. Objective v — comparative superiority

The eight paired differences span zero with no structure: three favour *M.
oleifera* (to −21.5 AUC-days), four favour *A. indica* (to +18.1), one is an
exact tie, and neither part nor parasite predicts the sign (@fig-forest;
@fig-paired). The paired test returns the null almost exactly (W = 14,
exact p = 1.0; HL 0.3, 95% CI −14.7 to 20.5; rank-biserial −0.14), and the
motility cross-check concurs (p = 0.15; @tbl-sup). Because the interval
covers meaningful effects in both directions, the data neither establish nor
exclude a modest plant difference — but as a superiority claim for either
agent, the answer is negative, and it is insensitive to any single block
(§6).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sup
#| tbl-cap: Plant superiority contrasts (paired Wilcoxon; 8 pairs each).
fmt_contrast("plant_superiority.csv")
fmt_contrast("plant_superiority_motility.csv")
```

![Paired AUC difference per block with overall HL estimate](`r file.path(fig_dir, "plant_forest.png")`){#fig-forest}

![Paired block-mean AUC scatter](`r file.path(fig_dir, "plant_paired_auc.png")`){#fig-paired}

## 6. Diagnostics, sensitivity and refits

Contrasts with tied ranks or zero differences report `n_nonzero`, `n_ties`
and the p-value method used (exact only when clean; continuity-corrected
normal approximation otherwise); refitting on this basis left no conclusion
changed. Paired differences were inspected for the symmetry the signed-rank
test assumes (@fig-sym): *evansi* differences form a pure location shift,
while the superiority differences are symmetric about zero, consistent with
its null. Leave-one-block-out re-analysis (@tbl-loo) found no conclusion
dependent on any single block. Completeness is asserted structurally at
build.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-loo
#| tbl-cap: Leave-one-block-out sensitivity (stable = no single block flips the conclusion).
k("sensitivity_loo.csv")
```

![Paired differences: symmetry check (red = median)](`r file.path(fig_dir, "diagnostic_paired_diffs.png")`){#fig-sym}

## 7. Discussion

Three assay layers converge on one finding: both extracts are genuinely and
dose-dependently trypanocidal. The in-vitro ordering (TTI 15 minutes to fully
censored across the dose range; @fig-tti) reappears quantitatively in peak
parasitaemia, mortality and cumulative burden (@tbl-peak, @fig-mort,
@fig-auc) — fast kill in the dish predicts low burden in the mouse — and the
Positive Controls trace the same rapid-kill profile, so the top extract dose
reproduces reference-like efficacy rather than merely beating an untreated
control. The most informative discordance is the effective threshold: full
immobilisation in-vitro demands ~100 mg/ml, yet *T. evansi* is suppressed
in-vivo from 0.5 mg/ml upward. Rather than a contradiction, this reflects the
assays' different sensitivities — ninety minutes of direct contact versus
forty days of systemic exposure with host clearance contributing — and it
locates the biologically interesting dose window for follow-up work between
0.5 and 10 mg/ml, particularly for *T. congolense*, whose threshold remains
unresolved. The two nulls sharpen the picture rather than weakening it. Plant
interchangeability, set against heavily overlapping phytochemistry (§5.2),
suggests the shared compound classes — or the shared extraction chemistry —
carry the activity, a hypothesis a fractionation study could test directly;
it also means formulation choice between these species can rest on cost,
toxicity and availability rather than efficacy. The weight/PCV nulls, finally,
do double duty: they rule out toxicity confounding of the parasitaemia
result and independently rank *T. congolense* the more pathogenic parasite.
What remains is confirmatory: animal-level (not group-mean) data with
identified controls, a refined dose grid around the *congolense* threshold,
and pre-registered block-level tests at adequate power — for which the
estimates and intervals in §5 provide the design inputs.

## 8. Limitations

Group means of three mice erase within-group variance, so inference rests on
sixteen blocks; intervals are wide and description carries the weight.
Control identities and doses are unknown, restricting the Positive Control
to a validity reference. Death-censored AUC flatters early-death groups and
is therefore always read with mortality. The NA-equals-death convention
awaits confirmation against animal records. All results are exploratory, not
confirmatory.
